$comment: RELEASE PARITY STATE. Enforced by scripts/release-parity-check.ts, which runs in CI and before a release. This file records, for every canonical migration at the release frontier, whether it is believed applied on the hosted database, and which database objects it introduces. The guard fails when application code on this branch references an object whose migration is not applied -- the exact class of failure that stopped employers saving jobs during UAT. It NEVER connects to a database, holds no credentials and applies no migration; it compares this repository against itself. Edit it deliberately: every entry is an owner-level statement about production.

frontier.note: EXPAND half of a two-phase release; the application half is 20261008090000 + the Career Journey code, which must NOT merge before this is applied. Consolidates the self-reported current profession into ONE canonical home: before this, security_career_profiles.current_profession_slug and sp_passport_profiles.cig_profession_slug were both user-writable, from two surfaces, with nothing keeping them in step. Adds a reconciliation log with least-privilege grants: SELECT on the table, COLUMN-LEVEL UPDATE (resolved_at) only, no INSERT and no DELETE, and an explicit REVOKE first because Supabase default privileges would otherwise grant all of them including TRUNCATE. Column-level because RLS constrains rows, not columns: a table-wide UPDATE would let a holder rewrite the canonical/passport values, the resolution or created_at on their own audit row, reconciles the existing rows under a rule that never overwrites a user own answer, and installs three sync triggers: canonical -> Passport mirror, seed of a newly created Passport row, and a temporary COMPATIBILITY trigger carrying an old client Passport write back to the canonical row. BACKWARD COMPATIBLE BY CONSTRUCTION: no column is dropped, no constraint is added that an existing client could violate, and the current application keeps writing exactly what it writes today -- proven statement-for-statement in Group F of supabase/tests/canonical_professional_profile_test.sql (54 assertions, full replay green). Safe to merge and apply with current main still running.

frontier.note: SCHEMA HALF of the AI CV. Private, owner-only storage for saved CV documents: presentation over facts that stay in security_career_profiles, sp_experience_periods, sp_claims and profiles, plus a snapshot of those facts so a saved CV does not silently change when the profile does. NO application code references cv_documents in this release -- that is the schema-first release contract working as designed, and schema-first-release-check asserts it. The save/load code becomes merge-eligible once this is recorded applied. Owner-only RLS with four separate policies (WITH CHECK on insert and update, so a row cannot be created for or reassigned to another person); privileges REVOKEd from PUBLIC/anon/authenticated first and re-granted to authenticated only, because Supabase default privileges otherwise ship anon INSERT/DELETE/TRUNCATE on any new table; anon gets nothing. No share token, no public column, no recipient table: a CV carries employment history and credentials and needs its own access model rather than the Career Card's. Writes no assertion_level, lifecycle_state, verified_at or verified_by_user_id -- it can create no verification. Verified locally: full db-test.sh replay green against the 54322 stack, including the 24 cv_documents assertions in supabase/tests/cv_documents_privacy_test.sql.

FUNCTION-ONLY. CREATE OR REPLACE on public.sp_verifier_decide, adding one guard: a decision of 'rejected' or 'clarification_requested' must carry a non-whitespace _holder_message. Introduces no object -- the function already exists (defined 20260817120000, replaced 20260818090000) -- and so does not gate the application release it ships with. Creates no table, no column, no policy and no new grant; the REVOKE/GRANT block is the existing one restated because CREATE OR REPLACE on a SECURITY DEFINER function is exactly where a grant silently widens. Adds no CHECK constraint to sp_verification_requests: rows decided before this migration may carry a null holder_message, they are immutable history, and a table constraint would need either a rewrite of that history or a NOT VALID exception that claims more than it enforces -- the function is the only route by which a request reaches those two states, since authenticated holds SELECT and INSERT on that table and no UPDATE. Rewrites no data. Does not touch approval, the self-verification bar, the verifier or employer-representative checks, the already-decided check, or the append-only decision log; the whole body is reproduced so a reviewer can see none of them moved. Safe in either deploy order -- applied before the code, an older reviewer form submitting a reasonless rejection is refused, which is the intended end state. Verified locally: full db-test.sh replay green against the 54322 stack, 67 Security Passport Phase 10 assertions including the new GROUP 10, which calls the RPC directly the way a crafted PostgREST call would and asserts the database is byte-for-byte unchanged after each refusal.
frontier.verify: SELECT prosrc LIKE '%SP_DECISION_REQUIRES_HOLDER_MESSAGE%' FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid = p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname='sp_verifier_decide';  -- expect t. Then: SELECT proacl FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname='sp_verifier_decide';  -- expect authenticated=X, and NO anon and no PUBLIC entry.

frontier.note: SECURITY. Closes three trust-boundary defects, all reachable over PostgREST without this application. (A) request_kind='employer_attestation' could name a CLAIM: a holder could open an employer attestation against a regulated credential such as VU1 and an owner/admin of the target employer could approve it, producing a state-regulated guard qualification 'verified' by a company with no standing to say so. Now refused at three points -- a new CHECK constraint sp_vr_employer_attestation_is_employment_only on sp_verification_requests (period_id NOT NULL AND claim_id IS NULL), a guard in sp_submit_for_verification, and a guard in sp_verifier_decide so a row written BEFORE this migration still cannot be turned into trust. (B) sp_verifier_decide accepted decision='approved' with verification_method NULL; only the TypeScript layer refused it, and that layer is skippable. Now refused in the function. WHICH methods are allowed is not restated: the existing sp_verification_requests.verification_method CHECK remains the model. (C) sp_verifier_decide read the request's status and then wrote with no lock across the gap, so two concurrent deciders could both pass the already-decided check and both write. The SELECT now takes FOR UPDATE on that one row, and a partial unique index sp_vd_one_final_decision_per_request makes 'one final decision per request' an invariant of the data (excludes clarification_requested, which is not final, and revoked, which is filed against the approving request on purpose). Two partial unique indexes sp_vr_one_open_request_per_claim / _per_period do the same for the matching submission race; sp_submit_for_verification maps the resulting unique violation back to SP_REQUEST_ALREADY_OPEN. Creates no table and no column, adds no workflow state, no assertion level and no verification method, and does not touch sp_is_verifier. Introduces no object the application calls, so it does not gate the application release it ships with. Rewrites no data: each new invariant is checked against existing rows in a preflight DO block that refuses with the offending identifiers rather than being added NOT VALID. Grants restated, not widened; anon still holds nothing. Verified locally against the 54322 stack: full strict replay of all 243 active migrations clean, 54 new trust-boundary assertions and 8 concurrent-decision assertions green, and the whole db-test.sh suite green. The concurrency fix is mutation-tested: with FOR UPDATE stripped the second decider still reached the INSERT and was caught by the new index, and with BOTH removed the original defect reproduced exactly -- two immutable decision rows and two Passport events for one request.
frontier.verify: SELECT conname FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='public.sp_verification_requests'::regclass AND conname='sp_vr_employer_attestation_is_employment_only';  -- expect 1 row. Then: SELECT indexname FROM pg_indexes WHERE schemaname='public' AND indexname IN ('sp_vd_one_final_decision_per_request','sp_vr_one_open_request_per_claim','sp_vr_one_open_request_per_period');  -- expect 3 rows. Then: SELECT prosrc LIKE '%SP_APPROVAL_REQUIRES_METHOD%', prosrc LIKE '%_request_id FOR UPDATE%', prosrc LIKE '%SP_DECISION_REQUIRES_HOLDER_MESSAGE%' FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname='sp_verifier_decide';  -- expect t|t|t. Then: SELECT proacl FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname IN ('sp_verifier_decide','sp_submit_for_verification');  -- expect authenticated=X, and NO anon and no PUBLIC entry.

frontier.note: SECURITY + FUNCTION-ONLY. (A) PRIVACY. sp_verification_requests.decision_note and sp_verification_decisions.decision_note are INTERNAL reviewer reasoning; the candidate is told holder_message. authenticated held TABLE-level SELECT on both tables and the holder's own RLS policies (sp_vr_self, sp_vd_read) match their rows, so the holder read the internal note simply by asking for it. Confirmed empirically before the fix against the local 54321/54322 stack with a real holder token over HTTP: GET /rest/v1/sp_verification_requests?select=decision_note and GET /rest/v1/sp_verification_decisions?select=decision_note each returned the note in full. The same table-level INSERT grant let a holder PLANT a decision_note on their own pending request, text that reaches the reviewer's detail payload looking like a colleague's reasoning; also confirmed. Fixed with COLUMN-level privileges: SELECT is re-granted on every column EXCEPT decision_note, and INSERT on sp_verification_requests is narrowed to the columns a holder legitimately supplies (id, holder_user_id, claim_id, period_id, request_kind, target_employer_id, status). NO RLS POLICY IS TOUCHED -- which rows a principal sees is unchanged, only which column. The three functions that legitimately read the note (sp_verifier_decide, sp_verifier_revoke, sp_verifier_request_detail) are all SECURITY DEFINER and run as the owner, so reviewer access is unaffected; nothing else in the repository selects the column. Column lists are explicit so a future column is unreadable until granted rather than readable until noticed. anon re-revoked rather than assumed, because this project's hosted database grants new objects to anon by default. After the fix the same crafted HTTP reads return 42501 permission denied -- including select=* -- while holder_message, status, decision, decider_organisation, verification_method and decided_at all still return normally. (B) REVIEWER DETAIL. sp_verifier_request_detail is rewritten ADDITIVELY: every key it returned it still returns, with the same name and type. Adds to 'claim' credential_code, credential_reference, sub_jurisdiction, authorisation_scope, holder_note and valid_from; adds to 'period' security_relevance, security_fraction, fte_fraction and version_no; and computes 'previous_versions' for employment periods, which was claim-only, so a period corrected by supersession no longer reaches the reviewer looking like a first submission. Creates no table and no column, rewrites no row, adds no workflow state, no assertion level and no verification method. Grants restated, not widened.
frontier.verify: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.column_privileges WHERE grantee='authenticated' AND table_name IN ('sp_verification_requests','sp_verification_decisions') AND column_name='decision_note' AND privilege_type='SELECT';  -- expect 0. Then: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE grantee='authenticated' AND table_name IN ('sp_verification_requests','sp_verification_decisions') AND privilege_type IN ('SELECT','INSERT');  -- expect 0 (table-level gone; privileges are column-level). Then: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.column_privileges WHERE grantee='authenticated' AND table_name='sp_verification_requests' AND column_name='holder_message' AND privilege_type='SELECT';  -- expect 1. Then: SELECT prosrc LIKE '%credential_reference%', prosrc LIKE '%sub_jurisdiction%', prosrc LIKE '%authorisation_scope%', prosrc LIKE '%sp_experience_periods pe%' FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname='sp_verifier_request_detail';  -- expect t|t|t|t.
SELECT 'passport_verifier' = ANY(enum_range(NULL::public.app_role)::text[]);  -- expect t.
frontier.note: ENUM-ONLY. Adds one value, 'passport_verifier', to public.app_role. Its own migration because PostgreSQL refuses to USE a newly added enum value in the transaction that adds it, and 20261016090000 reads it inside sp_is_verifier and inside the admin_set_platform_role allowlist -- a single combined file fails to apply with 'unsafe use of new value of enum type'. Creates no table, no column, no policy, no grant and no function, and rewrites no data. Grants nobody anything on its own: until a user_roles row carries the value AND 20261016090000 teaches sp_is_verifier to read it, this changes no authorization decision anywhere. Safe in either deploy order. Not reversible by ALTER TYPE (PostgreSQL has no DROP VALUE); the rollback file documents why an inert enum value is left in place rather than rewriting public.user_roles to remove it.

frontier.verify: SELECT prosrc LIKE '%passport_verifier%' FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname='sp_is_verifier';  -- expect t. Then: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.role_table_grants WHERE table_schema='public' AND table_name LIKE 'sp\_%' AND grantee IN ('anon','authenticated') AND privilege_type IN ('TRUNCATE','REFERENCES','TRIGGER');  -- expect 0. Then: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.column_privileges WHERE grantee='authenticated' AND table_name IN ('sp_verification_requests','sp_verification_decisions') AND column_name='decided_by' AND privilege_type='SELECT';  -- expect 0. Then: SELECT count(*) FROM information_schema.column_privileges WHERE grantee='authenticated' AND table_name='sp_verification_decisions' AND column_name='decider_organisation' AND privilege_type='SELECT';  -- expect 1. Then: SELECT proacl FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname IN ('sp_is_verifier','admin_set_platform_role');  -- expect authenticated=X, and NO anon and no PUBLIC entry.
frontier.note: SECURITY. (A) ROLE SEPARATION. public.sp_is_verifier was defined as, literally, 'SELECT public.is_platform_admin(_user_id)'. Every Passport reviewer path in the database funnels through it -- sp_verifier_queue, sp_verifier_request_detail, sp_verifier_decide, sp_verifier_revoke, dispute resolution, the evidence storage policy and three RLS policies -- so the only way to let somebody review a credential was to make them a platform admin, which also confers user administration, employer administration, jobs, applications, assessments, audit and permanent account deletion. Now: has_role(user,'passport_verifier') OR is_platform_admin(user). The OR is one-directional and deliberate: every existing platform admin keeps reviewing with nothing re-granted, while a passport_verifier is NOT an admin -- is_platform_admin() is untouched, still reads admin/superadmin only, and every admin-gated surface refuses a reviewer. No new subsystem: public.user_roles is already the platform's server-side, service-role-managed, RLS-protected role store with granted_at/granted_by, and admin_set_platform_role() is already the sole audited superadmin-only grant/revoke path -- its hard allowlist is widened from ('admin','superadmin') by exactly one value and nothing else in it changes. (B) TRUNCATE. This project's hosted database carries ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES IN SCHEMA public GRANT ALL ON TABLES TO anon, authenticated, so every Passport table arrived with the full privilege set. Six of the seven are bounded by RLS; TRUNCATE is not bounded by anything, because row-level security does not apply to TRUNCATE at all. Verified empirically before the fix on a disposable replay of the whole migration history with the hosted default privileges applied FIRST -- a clean local replay cannot show this, because the migrations that mirror those defaults (20260817190000/20260817210000/20260916090000) are timestamped after the Passport tables were created: BEGIN; SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated; TRUNCATE public.sp_verification_decisions; returned TRUNCATE TABLE. That is the append-only decision log -- the entire immutable record of who verified what, by what method -- emptied by any signed-in user. 21 sp_ tables were exposed, sp_pilot_members to anon as well. PostgREST never issues TRUNCATE so it was not reachable through the Data API, but the grant was real. TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER are now revoked from anon and authenticated on every sp_ table; after the fix the same statement returns 42501. SELECT/INSERT/DELETE are untouched. UPDATE on both verification tables and INSERT on the decision log are also revoked: unlike TRUNCATE these were already refused (RLS does bound them and neither table carries such a policy), and they are removed so the append-only guarantee does not depend on the continued absence of a policy. Nothing in the repository writes either table directly; every write is a SECURITY DEFINER function running as the owner. (C) decided_by. Migration 20261014090000's column-SELECT lists included decided_by, so a holder could read the internal user id of the individual person who judged their credential. Revoked on both tables. decider_organisation, decision, verification_method, decided_at and holder_message all stay granted, and are what the candidate-facing panel already renders -- nothing candidate-facing in this repository selects decided_by, so no product path regresses. The COLUMN IS NOT DROPPED and no row is rewritten: the internal audit trail keeps decided_by in full, and the SECURITY DEFINER verifier functions that read it are unaffected because they run as the owner. SCOPE. The revoke is scoped to sp_ tables and the ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES statements themselves are deliberately NOT changed -- altering them would silently change every future table in the schema, including domains this pass has not audited. Recorded as a deferred finding instead. Creates no table and no column, adds no trust state, no assertion level and no verification method, touches no RLS policy, and rewrites no data. The migration asserts its own end state in the same transaction (privilege leak, decided_by, provenance survival, decision_note regression, capability wiring) and raises rather than returning, so a partial application rolls back. Verified locally against the 54322 stack: full strict replay of the active migration history clean, and 57 new reviewer-role and least-privilege assertions green, each executed as the authenticated principal rather than read from a policy listing.

frontier.verify: SELECT prosrc LIKE '%''is_self''%', prosrc LIKE '%a.display_name%', prosrc LIKE '%SP_NOT_EMPLOYER_REPRESENTATIVE%' FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname='sp_employer_attestation_queue';  -- expect t|t|t. Then: SELECT prosrc LIKE '%sp_claims%', prosrc LIKE '%sp_evidence%', prosrc LIKE '%decision_note%' FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname='sp_employer_attestation_queue';  -- expect f|f|f. Then: SELECT proacl FROM pg_proc p JOIN pg_namespace n ON n.oid=p.pronamespace WHERE n.nspname='public' AND p.proname='sp_employer_attestation_queue';  -- expect authenticated=X, and NO anon and no PUBLIC entry. Then: SELECT conname FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid='public.sp_verification_requests'::regclass AND conname='sp_vr_employer_attestation_is_employment_only';  -- expect 1 row, unchanged by this migration.
frontier.note: FUNCTION-ONLY. Rewrites public.sp_employer_attestation_queue and nothing else -- no table, no column, no policy, no index, no constraint, no grant change, no trust state, no workflow state, no assertion level and no verification method. Rewrites no row. PR 8 makes an existing capability FINDABLE (the employer-facing surface moves into the employer workspace and is surfaced on their overview); the only part of that which the database has to answer is here. (A) is_self. A candidate may also be an owner or admin of the company they worked for, which is an ordinary career and not an abuse. has_employer_role() is true for them, so their own request appeared in their own employer queue with a Confirm control beside it -- and pressing it produced an unexplained failure, because sp_verifier_decide refuses on _r.holder_user_id = auth.uid() before it writes anything. The refusal was correct; offering the control was not. The queue now returns is_self, computed from auth.uid() in the database, so the surface can state the refusal in advance rather than staging it. THIS IS NOT A PERMISSION and does not become one: the bar remains in sp_verifier_decide, untouched, and the suite proves both an approval and a rejection by the dual-role principal are still refused with SP_SELF_VERIFICATION_FORBIDDEN and write nothing. sp_verifier_queue has returned the equivalent flag since Phase 10 for exactly this reason. (B) holder_name fallback. The field read sp_passport_profiles.display_name, which is NULLABLE, and coalesced it to ''. An employer was then shown a role and a date range with no person named and asked whether it was correct -- not a harder question but an unanswerable one. It now falls back to public.profiles.display_name (the account's own name, set by the same person) before the empty string. This adds no NEW CATEGORY of information to a payload whose first field was always the holder's name, is reachable only because the function is SECURITY DEFINER and has already proved the caller is an owner or admin of the employer the request names, and is the same fallback scp_employer_team already makes for the same reason. SCOPE UNCHANGED. The authorisation check (has_employer_role owner|admin, raising SP_NOT_EMPLOYER_REPRESENTATIVE) stays first and unchanged; the field list stays an explicit list, so a column added to any joined table is invisible here until written in. The function still cannot reach sp_claims, sp_evidence or decision_note, and returns no contact details -- asserted in the migration itself and again in the suite by EXECUTING the reads as the employer principal rather than reading policies. Grants restated rather than assumed, because CREATE OR REPLACE on a SECURITY DEFINER function is exactly where a grant widens unnoticed on this project's hosted database, whose default privileges grant every new object to anon; the migration asserts its own end state (both new keys present, authorisation intact, no widened read, anon holds no EXECUTE, authenticated still holds it) and raises rather than returning, so a partial application rolls back. DEPLOY ORDER: additive to the returned JSON in both directions, safe in either order. Applied first, the current application ignores the two new keys; applied after the code, is_self is absent and the mapper reads it as false -- which is today's behaviour exactly, and the decision was always refused by the database rather than by the flag. Verified locally against the 54322 stack: full db-test.sh green, including 73 new employer employment verification assertions covering the narrow read, the unrelated-organisation refusal, the ordinary-member refusal, the dual-role self-confirmation refusal with a before/after record fingerprint, the mandatory candidate-facing message on both refusal outcomes, one-final-decision, one-open-request, decision_note privacy, and the fact that an employer who says the dates are wrong still cannot change them.
